What is the most appropriate response?
answers: Move the mission-critical services to a dedicated ArcGIS Server site and route requests to it
Add another machine to the shared site so that all services get more capacity during the surges
Lower the maximum instances for every service on the shared site to cap resource use
Ask general staff to avoid using GIS services whenever an emergency is declared
questions.explanation: Esri lists mission-critical services with a higher SLA as a workload that benefits from isolation on a separate site, which reduces the chance that a spike in other requests disrupts them. Adding a machine to the shared site still leaves the emergency services competing with the surge for the same resources.

source.title: ArcGIS Architecture Center: Workload separation

questions.objective: Determine when to use workload separation
questions.question: An architect has split a deployment into separate ArcGIS Server sites for hosting, mapping and analytics. The network team asks how user requests should reach the correct site while protecting each site from overload on the others. Following Esri guidance, what should you recommend?
answers: Route user requests to the appropriate ArcGIS Server site through load balancers
Use DNS round robin to spread requests evenly across every machine in all sites
Expose port 6443 on each ArcGIS Server machine so clients can connect directly
Rejoin all machines into one site and let round robin decide where requests go
questions.explanation: Esri recommends routing user requests to the appropriate ArcGIS Server sites through load balancers, which stops overloaded machines affecting other machines. Spreading requests across all machines, or rejoining the sites, would undo the separation.

source.title: ArcGIS Architecture Center: Workload separation

questions.objective: Determine when to use workload separation
questions.question: Workload separation is now in place for a utility's ArcGIS Enterprise deployment. The GIS manager expects usage to grow over the next two years and asks how the team will know when the separation design needs to change. Which approach aligns with Esri's workload separation strategy?
answers: Set acceptable component thresholds, monitor against them and adapt before they are exceeded
Wait until users report slow performance, then move the affected services to a new site
Size every site now for three times today's peak load and leave the design unchanged
Review the separation design only when ArcGIS Enterprise is next upgraded to a new major release
questions.explanation: Esri's strategy is to determine acceptable component thresholds, plan for expected load and monitor components so you can adapt proactively when thresholds are approached. Waiting for user complaints is reactive and contradicts the guidance to identify rising utilisation early.

source.title: ArcGIS Architecture Center: Workload separation
source.section: Strategies for workload separation; Measure success

questions.objective: Design system based on environment isolation needs
questions.question: A newly hired architect proposes separate development, QA, performance-test, training, staging and production ArcGIS Enterprise environments, saying 'that's how my last organisation did it'. The project sponsor is concerned about cost. What is the most appropriate response?
answers: Weigh the resource, licensing and staff costs against risk tolerance and present them for decision
Approve all six environments, because adding more isolated environments always lowers risk to production users
Remove every non-production environment and test all changes in production outside business hours
Host staging and production on the same machines so the organisation can keep every environment
questions.explanation: Esri notes that environment isolation has real costs (IT resources, licensing and staff), so the costs should be investigated and explained to stakeholders, letting them make an informed decision rather than defaulting to 'we have always done it that way'. More environments are not automatically justified.

source.title: ArcGIS Architecture Center: Environment isolation
source.section: Benefits and costs of environment isolation

questions.objective: Design system based on environment isolation needs
questions.question: An agency runs an enterprise application hosting system that delivers business-critical web apps to thousands of staff. A business unit asks for content creator privileges in production so it can build and adjust Experience Builder apps directly where users access them. What is the most appropriate response?
answers: Have them build apps in a lower environment and promote them through a change-controlled process
Grant production privileges and rely on unshared items to hide their work in progress from users
Grant production privileges but restrict their app building to after business hours
Let them build in production, then copy each finished app to staging for a review
questions.explanation: In the enterprise application hosting and management pattern, app building is not used in production; apps are built in lower environments and promoted to production through a change-controlled process. Hiding unshared work in production still exposes the live system to unmanaged change.

source.title: ArcGIS Architecture Center: Enterprise application hosting and management overview

questions.objective: Design system based on environment isolation needs
questions.question: Administrators configure the staging and production ArcGIS Enterprise environments by hand from a written runbook. The two have drifted, and a change that passed testing in staging failed in production. What should the team do to make the environments consistent?
answers: Automate deployment and configuration with scripts and tools, developing the scripts in development
Require a second administrator to check each manual step in the runbook before the change is signed off
Retire staging, because it no longer matches production and its test results are unreliable
Apply every change to production first, then copy production settings back to staging
questions.explanation: Esri recommends avoiding manual configuration to reduce human error, using tools such as PowerShell DSC for ArcGIS, the ArcGIS REST API and the ArcGIS API for Python, and notes that creating these scripts is an activity for the development environment. Peer review still leaves a manual, error-prone process.

source.title: ArcGIS Architecture Center: Environment isolation

questions.objective: Determine which type of collaboration to use based on requirements
questions.question: Your internal-only ArcGIS Enterprise 11.4 portal is a guest in a partner agency's ArcGIS Online-hosted collaboration. You shared a map image layer from a federated server to the workspace group, but partner users cannot open it because they cannot reach your network. The data must still reach them. What should you do?
answers: Share the data as a sync-enabled feature layer to a workspace that shares feature layers as copies
Reconfigure the workspace to share as copies so that the map image layer is copied to the partner
Share the map image layer with Everyone in your portal so partner users no longer need to sign in
Ask the host to change your access mode to Send and Receive so that the partner can open the layer
questions.explanation: ArcGIS Server services such as map image layers are shared only by reference, so recipients must be able to reach the original service; sync-enabled feature layers can be shared as copies and hosted in the recipient's organisation. Changing the workspace to copies does not copy a map image layer.

source.title: ArcGIS Enterprise 11.4: Share content with collaboration participants
source.section: Share layers and views; Share ArcGIS Server services

questions.objective: Determine which type of collaboration to use based on requirements
questions.question: A council and its maintenance contractor share asset layers as copies with two-way edits enabled. Both organisations' field crews may edit the same assets on the same day. The contractor's GIS lead asks how conflicting edits are handled. What is the most accurate answer?
answers: No conflict check occurs and the last edit submitted overwrites, so agree who edits which features
The host organisation's edits always take precedence over edits made in a guest organisation
Conflicting edits are held in a queue until the layer owner reconciles them in ArcGIS Pro
The next synchronisation rejects any edits that conflict and flags them for review by both organisations
questions.explanation: Esri cautions that no checks occur to detect or prevent concurrent edits in two-way sharing; the last change submitted takes precedence, so editing responsibilities should be managed and the archive consulted. There is no host-wins rule or reconcile queue.

source.title: ArcGIS Enterprise 11.4: Share content with collaboration participants

questions.objective: Determine which type of collaboration to use based on requirements
questions.question: A department's ArcGIS Enterprise 11.4 portal is already a guest in a collaboration hosted by the city's ArcGIS Online organisation. A regional body now invites the department to join a second distributed collaboration hosted by the regional body's own ArcGIS Online organisation. What is the most appropriate response?
answers: Explain the portal can collaborate with only one ArcGIS Online organisation at a time
Accept the invitation, because each ArcGIS Online-hosted collaboration is independent of any others
Host the second collaboration from the department's portal and invite the regional organisation
Accept, but set the second collaboration's workspace to Receive only so that it does not conflict
questions.explanation: An ArcGIS Enterprise organisation can only collaborate with one ArcGIS Online organisation at a time. Hosting from the portal is not an option either, because the ArcGIS Online organisation must be the host in any collaboration that includes it.

source.title: ArcGIS Enterprise 11.4: Set up an ArcGIS Enterprise and ArcGIS Online collaboration

questions.objective: Determine which type of collaboration to use based on requirements
questions.question: The administrator of an ArcGIS Online organisation hosting a collaboration wants each ArcGIS Enterprise guest's feature layer copies refreshed every 30 minutes, and plans to set this schedule centrally for all guests. What is the most appropriate response?
answers: Ask each guest administrator to set the workspace schedule, noting that the shortest interval is one hour
Set the 30-minute schedule in the host's workspace settings so that it applies to every guest at the same time
Set the 30-minute schedule on each guest's linked group from the host organisation's group settings
Change each guest's access mode to Receive so that the host can control the schedule for that guest
questions.explanation: Guests control the sync schedule for each workspace; the host does not. Scheduled sync can run every 1–24 hours, so 30 minutes is not available as a scheduled interval. Receive-only guests do not see the sync options at all.

source.title: ArcGIS Enterprise 11.4: Configure sync settings

questions.objective: Apply procedural concepts to identify a content delivery strategy
questions.question: A public web app built with the ArcGIS Maps SDK for JavaScript draws a hosted feature layer from ArcGIS Enterprise 11.4. Traffic is high, the data is edited daily and users must be able to click features to see pop-ups. Which caching approach best fits these requirements?
answers: Enable response caching on the layer so that standard tile queries are cached in the object store
Republish the data as a cached map image layer and rebuild its raster tile cache every night after editing
Place a CDN in front of the portal and cache the layer's REST query responses at the edge
Turn off the layer's pop-ups and query capability so that each request costs the server less
questions.explanation: In ArcGIS Enterprise, response caching is enabled per layer, stores cached responses in the object store and is used by clients such as the ArcGIS Maps SDK for JavaScript, while keeping the layer queryable. Raster tiles do not allow users to identify features, and Esri advises against caching dynamic REST responses in a CDN.

source.title: ArcGIS Architecture Center: Optimize performance in ArcGIS

questions.objective: Apply procedural concepts to identify a content delivery strategy
questions.question: A council has a new high-resolution aerial orthophoto mosaic, refreshed every two years. It will be the background in most of the council's web apps, and no one needs to analyse or restyle it. The GIS team is choosing how to deliver it. Which option best fits Esri guidance?
answers: Publish it as a cached tile layer of pre-rendered raster tiles
Publish it as a vector tile layer with a client-side style
Serve it as a dynamic image service drawn on every request
Serve it as a feature layer with query response caching
questions.explanation: Raster tile caching suits relatively static data viewed in one cartographic representation, and raster tiles are still used for many imagery basemaps based on satellite or orthophotography. Vector tiles store vector geometry and attributes, so they do not suit an imagery backdrop.

source.title: ArcGIS Architecture Center: Optimize performance in ArcGIS
source.section: Strategies for map image layer caching

questions.objective: Apply procedural concepts to identify a content delivery strategy
questions.question: A developer proposes a CDN, a full raster tile cache and reverse-proxy response caching for a new internal app that six analysts will use a few times a day. The GIS manager asks whether this effort is justified. What is the most appropriate response?
answers: Scale the optimisation to the audience; focus on the app being useful and performing well for the analysts
Proceed, because every ArcGIS resource should be optimised to handle thousands of requests per second
Proceed, but publish the app in ArcGIS Online instead so that it can make use of Esri's built-in global CDN
Skip all testing, because an app with only six users cannot have performance or usability problems
questions.explanation: Esri advises that user needs should decide which optimisations are worthwhile: a resource used a few times a day by a small internal group does not need to scale to thousands of requests per second, though the same optimisation could be vital for a global public audience. Usefulness and structured testing still matter.

source.title: ArcGIS Architecture Center: Optimize performance in ArcGIS

questions.objective: Identify methods for backup, replication and/or resiliency
questions.question: Asset editors work in an enterprise geodatabase through feature services that reference it. The business has set an RPO of one hour for these edits. The backup team runs only a nightly WebGISDR backup. What is the most appropriate response?
answers: Have the DBA back up the geodatabase with DBMS tools at a cadence shorter than one hour
Run WebGISDR in incremental mode every hour so that it also captures the geodatabase edits
Take hourly VM snapshots of the running database server as the main backup method
Keep the nightly WebGISDR backup, because referenced data is included in its output
questions.explanation: WebGISDR does not back up referenced data sources; enterprise geodatabases should be backed up with the database vendor's tools according to the RPO (Esri gives the example of incremental geodatabase backups every 15 minutes). Hourly WebGISDR runs, incremental or not, still would not include the geodatabase.

source.title: ArcGIS Enterprise 11.4: Back up and restore best practices
source.section: Back up referenced data sources; When to back up

questions.objective: Identify methods for backup, replication and/or resiliency
questions.question: After a storage failure, an organisation must rebuild its whole ArcGIS Enterprise deployment and the enterprise geodatabases and file shares it references. The service desk wants the portal restored first so that staff can sign in as soon as possible. What restore order does Esri recommend?
answers: Restore the referenced databases and file shares first and verify access, then restore ArcGIS Enterprise
Restore Portal for ArcGIS first so that staff can sign in, then the federated servers and finally the databases
Restore every component at the same time to minimise the total recovery time for the organisation
Restore ArcGIS Enterprise first, then the referenced data sources, and republish affected services
questions.explanation: Esri recommends making all referenced data sources available first and verifying that ArcGIS Enterprise can reach them, then restoring ArcGIS Enterprise to a consistent state. Restoring the portal first risks items and services that point to data that is not yet available.

source.title: ArcGIS Enterprise 11.4: Back up and restore best practices

questions.objective: Identify methods for backup, replication and/or resiliency
questions.question: A faulty script made bad edits yesterday to a hosted feature layer stored in the ArcGIS Data Store relational store. Everything else in the deployment is healthy. The GIS manager suggests restoring last night's full WebGISDR backup over the whole deployment. What is the most appropriate response?
answers: Restore only the relational data store, checking for any hosted services published since the backup
Restore the full WebGISDR backup, because it is the only supported way to roll back hosted data
Restore the enterprise geodatabase backup from last night, because it holds hosted feature data
Restore yesterday's VM snapshot of the portal machine, because it contains the hosted layer data
questions.explanation: Esri notes that bad edits to a hosted feature layer can be rolled back by restoring only the relational data store, which limits impact, although hosted services created in the meantime may need manual clean-up and republishing. Hosted data is in the relational data store, not in a user-managed enterprise geodatabase.

source.title: ArcGIS Enterprise 11.4: Back up and restore best practices

questions.objective: Identify methods for backup, replication and/or resiliency
questions.question: A deployment includes ArcGIS GeoEvent Server and a graph store registered with the hosting server. The backup lead says the nightly WebGISDR export covers 'everything in ArcGIS Enterprise'. What is the most appropriate response?
answers: Add separate backups: the GeoEvent configuration file and backupdatastore for the graph store
Agree, as WebGISDR backs up all federated servers and all ArcGIS Data Store types
Set WebGISDR to full mode, because full mode adds the GeoEvent and graph store data
Agree for GeoEvent Server, but add VM snapshots of the graph store machines to cover them
questions.explanation: WebGISDR backups exclude the GeoEvent Server site configuration (back it up with its configuration file) and graph and spatiotemporal big data stores (back them up with the ArcGIS Data Store backupdatastore utility). Full mode contains the same content as backup mode.

source.title: ArcGIS Enterprise 11.4: Back up and restore ArcGIS Enterprise

questions.objective: Given a scenario, determine when to use tiered architectures
questions.question: The DBA team is making the SQL Server instance behind a registered enterprise geodatabase highly available, with automatic failover to a secondary server. The GIS team asks how ArcGIS Server should connect so that a database failover does not break its services. What is the most appropriate recommendation?
answers: Register the database using a DNS alias or flexible IP that always points to the active server
Register the primary server by host name and re-register the data store after any failover
Register both database servers as separate data stores and publish each service twice
Copy the data into the ArcGIS Data Store relational store, which has its own failover built in
questions.explanation: Esri notes that ArcGIS can work with database HA configurations when data is registered through a DNS alias or flexible IP that may point to a different backend database after an outage, so ArcGIS components are unaware of the change. Re-registering after each failover adds manual downtime that the alias avoids.

source.title: ArcGIS Architecture Center: High availability

questions.objective: Given a scenario, determine when to use tiered architectures
questions.question: To save costs on a new highly available ArcGIS Enterprise deployment, the infrastructure manager proposes using ArcGIS Web Adaptor as the only load balancer, with no third-party load balancer in the web tier. What is the most appropriate response?
answers: Include at least one third-party load balancer, which can route traffic through the Web Adaptor
Accept, because Web Adaptor detects healthy machines and can act as the sole load balancer
Accept, but install Web Adaptor on both of the portal machines so the web tier has two load balancers
Remove Web Adaptor and use DNS round robin across the portal and server machines for failover
questions.explanation: Esri states that at least one third-party load balancer is required in a highly available ArcGIS Enterprise deployment, and that Web Adaptor is inadequate as the lone load balancer. Web Adaptor can still be used behind it for security or web-tier authentication.

questions.objective: Given a scenario, determine when to use tiered architectures
questions.question: As part of a cloud migration, the cloud team will move the ArcGIS Enterprise machines to an IaaS region. The DBA wants the enterprise geodatabase that the federated services read and edit to stay in the on-premises data centre, connected over the WAN, and notes that the link has plenty of bandwidth. What is the most appropriate response?
answers: Keep ArcGIS Server and its database in the same network zone, and test any proposed split first
Accept, because high bandwidth on the link means the database traffic will perform as well as now
Accept, because browser clients are tolerant of network constraints, so service users will not notice
Accept, but move the ArcGIS Pro editors to the cloud too, as only desktop traffic is latency-sensitive
questions.explanation: Esri recommends hosting clients, server processes, storage and databases in the same network zone, notes that ArcGIS Server-to-database traffic needs low latency, and says latency matters more than bandwidth for day-to-day work; any split should be validated through structured testing. Browser tolerance does not remove the server-to-database latency.
